title: Which backup can fill this form?

beats.say: This access form needs an evidence ID. The primary timed out before it sent a word. Here is a sample from backup F. Slide its reply up to the empty field. F is healthy, handles private notes, and fits the budget. Would you send it this request?

Skip F. Its sample is a sentence. The form needs a separate field for evidence IDs and a way to send the case to a reviewer. Look at D's sample. It has both, in the required format. D still has to fit the time and money left.

The desk sends the same request whichever model it uses. The gateway chooses an approved path. If it sends the request to D, the adapter translates it into the model's format and translates the reply back. The model, its adapter, and the controls around them make up a lane.

Rewind to the record the desk sent. The private notes set the data boundary. An access decision needs a cited form. Nine hundred dollars of risk crosses the five-hundred-dollar review threshold. Clip the review requirement to the same record.

The input takes twenty-four thousand tokens. The policy screens each lane's estimated cost against half a cent. Taken together, those requirements are the contract. The lane prices and times in this exercise are teaching figures.

Suppose the router returned a private lane the moment it saw the notes. It would never reach the risk check. The desk could get a private answer with nowhere to send it for review. Keep the risk requirement alongside privacy when you choose the lane.

Now a client labels the request public and turns citations off. The trusted record still says access decision. That task requires private handling and citations. In a live service, authenticate the caller and authorize the task for this tenant before you compile the requirements from server-owned facts.

title: Each lane must satisfy the complete contract

beats.say: Lay the contract across all six lanes. A misses the private boundary, input size, citations, and review. B can fill the form but still fails privacy. Read across each row. Which lanes pass every field?
C, D, and E pass. These are the lanes we can rank.

Inspect the cheap text lane. Its data flag and price look acceptable, but schema, citations, and review fail. Lower cost cannot repair those missing capabilities. Keeping each failed field lets an operator explain exactly why the gateway rejected F.

Increase the private input to seventy thousand tokens. Compare that figure with the capacity printed on each row. No lane survives. Escalate with the input intact. At dispatch, count each lane's serialized input and reserve room for its output. Recheck region, retention, credentials, and the registry revision against the full policy.

Bring back the original input. Three lanes can do this job. With cost as our preference, compare their estimates. C is the cheapest. It gets the first call. If prices tied, this router would use time and then the lane ID to break the tie.

Suppose a new measurement puts D at seven hundred milliseconds. Its price stays where it was. Now the desk cares most about how soon the complete reply will arrive. Which approved lane should go first for speed?

Send D first. Its time is shorter than C's, although C still costs less. A learned router can use evidence from your own cases to rank these three. To admit a lane, test the model and adapter together.

Try the combination on a private test case. Can the adapter return the required schema with an evidence ID and deliver it to review? Keep those results with the model, adapter, and policy revisions. A shared request format alone tells us little about those behaviors. Measure the quality of the answers those lanes actually return.

title: Should R900 get a second attempt?

beats.say: Return to the original registry. D needs eleven hundred milliseconds. Start one clock for the whole request. C times out at nine hundred forty, before any output. There is one attempt left. With funding available, D runs on the same clock. It finishes at two thousand forty milliseconds.
That leaves four hundred sixty milliseconds before the deadline. Keep this completed run on the upper track.

Keep that first run in place. Replay the same request with one change. This time C takes eighteen hundred milliseconds to time out. Look at the space left before the deadline. We still have a generation attempt and funding for D. Would you start it?

Skip D. Lay its eleven hundred milliseconds after the timeout. It would finish at twenty-nine hundred, four hundred milliseconds past the deadline. The outline is work we considered. Only C ran. The regional backup needs even longer, so return the reason to the desk at eighteen hundred.

In production, queues, retry delays, and adapter work also use this clock. Replay the early timeout. Suppose all eligible backups share a provider that requires a two-second wait. Only fifteen hundred sixty milliseconds remain. Escalate now. Even the wait would cross the deadline.

Replay the early timeout. C's bill has settled at point four two cents. Lower the whole request cap from one cent to point eight cents. D needs half a cent reserved before it can start. Does that fit?

Only point three eight cents remain. Skip D. An estimated price helps rank the lanes. Before dispatch, reserve enough for the most the call can cost. Settle against actual usage when the bill arrives. A provider may keep working after a timeout, so hold its reservation until you know the charge.

Look at the user's response window. A timeout before the first word permits another generation attempt if the other checks pass. A temporary throttle can qualify too. An authentication failure, an exhausted quota, or a policy refusal stops this route. Changing providers cannot authorize the request.

Replay the call with streaming enabled. The user reads, “Your access request.” Now the connection drops. Those three words are already on the user's screen. End the partial reply, explain the interruption, and offer an explicit retry or handoff. Quietly appending D's reply could contradict what the user just read.

On a separate call, D has filled in the form. Before releasing it, compare its citation with the evidence this user may read. D cites E ninety-nine. The authorized passage is E one. Withhold this reply. The desk still has to explain why it held the reply.

Try a fresh buffered reply. This one cites E one. Read the passage beside it. The passage says a reviewer must approve viewer access. It supports sending the request for review. A matching ID by itself could also point to an unrelated passage. Confirm the case reached the review queue. The authorized human still decides whether to grant access.

title: When can C take another call?

beats.say: The desk has another request. How do we keep it from paying for the same sick primary? Count one timeout against C. A second timeout comes a second later. Now its circuit breaker opens for ten seconds. Ordinary calls skip C during that cooldown.
Follow the compatible lanes in order. If both C and D are open, a healthy, funded E can take the call if it fits the deadline.

Return to C. At eleven seconds the cooldown ends. The first arriving request, P one, takes the single probe permit. The circuit is half open while it tests C. P two arrives before that probe has returned. Can P two call C?

P two has to skip C. One probe is already in flight. When that probe succeeds, the circuit closes. A failed or expired probe would reopen it. Across workers, acquire the permit atomically and ignore stale results. Give the waiting clients a retry window.

Each draws its own delay under a bounded exponential ceiling. Here the first window runs from zero to two hundred milliseconds. Look at the three different waits. On the next retry the ceiling doubles, up to a configured cap. Honor any applicable retry delay, count the wait against the shared deadline, and limit how much traffic you admit.

Replay three cases before promoting a policy. A healthy primary serves the first. An early timeout sends the second to D. The oversized request escalates without calling anyone. Both served routes pass the contract checks. For each one, check the reviewed answer, the passages that support it, and what the provider charged.

Consider a separate case where a human already approved the grant. Operation G twenty-seven gave the user viewer access and stored a receipt. Only the explanation timed out. Pass the verified receipt into the next generation attempt.

If the write service receives the same operation key, it checks authorization again and compares the parameters. For the same authorized grant it returns the stored receipt. The grant count stays at one. A different target needs a new decision. Even with fresh approval for project forty-three, this key belongs to the grant for forty-two. The write service reports a conflict. A durable service must record the effect and its receipt together or reconcile them.

On the run where D had time and funding, both calls incurred a charge. The primary timed out. The local backup returned the reply. C cost point four two cents. We reserved half a cent for D. Its final charge was point four five cents.

Together they cost point eight seven cents. Price each provider's reported usage on its own rate card. Keep both attempts with the policy and registry revisions. Both charges belong to the explanation. The receipt records one grant.

Replay the explanation with a new timeout. The grant is already on file. The requirements and funding are the same, and the user has seen no words. C times out after thirteen hundred ninety-nine milliseconds. D still needs eleven hundred.
Our policy admits a backup only when its expected finish is strictly before the deadline. Use the start time and D's run time. Would you send D?
Add them. The finish is twenty-four hundred ninety-nine milliseconds. That's one tick inside the line. Send D. In this replay the reply arrives on that tick. The desk can now check it before release.
Keep D and the deadline fixed. Move C's timeout one tick later, to fourteen hundred milliseconds. The green dot marks the first run. Make the dispatch decision again.

This finish lands exactly at twenty-five hundred. D had to finish before that tick. Skip D. The regional backup is slower still, so the gateway stops at fourteen hundred milliseconds after one attempt. The support agent gets the timeout and the grant receipt. Viewer access was granted. Only the explanation timed out.
